title: Dynamic Secrets: Credentials That Don't Exist Until You Ask
intro: A stored password is the same for everyone, lives for years, and can't be traced to whoever used it. Vault's database secrets engine does the opposite: on request it creates a brand-new database user with a short lifetime, hands it over, and deletes it when the lease ends. The engine is mounted at database/, with a role named shop-readonly.

steps.prompt: Ask Vault for database credentials from the role shop-readonly.
steps.fake_output:
Key                Value
---                -----
lease_id           database/creds/shop-readonly/kQx7TnB2hVp9
lease_duration     1h
lease_renewable    true
password           A1a-Zq9vXw3RtLm7example
username           v-oidc-dana-shop-read-8f2Kq1
steps.explanation: Vault just created a database user that didn't exist a second ago, valid for one hour.
steps.why: The username records who asked (your OIDC identity) and through which role, so the database's own logs show a person, not a shared account. Each caller gets different credentials, so one being leaked or revoked affects nobody else. And nothing needs rotating: the credential expires by itself.

steps.prompt: Confirm the user really exists in the database: list role names starting with v-oidc in PostgreSQL.
expected_commands: psql -c "SELECT rolname, rolvaliduntil FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname LIKE 'v-oidc%';"
psql -c "SELECT rolname, rolvaliduntil FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname LIKE 'v-oidc%'"
psql -c "SELECT rolname FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname LIKE 'v-oidc%';"
steps.hint: SELECT rolname, rolvaliduntil FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname LIKE 'v-oidc%';
steps.explanation: A real PostgreSQL role, with an expiry an hour from now.
steps.why: Vault holds one privileged database account and uses it to run CREATE ROLE and, later, DROP ROLE. So that one account is the thing to protect, and Vault can rotate its password itself ('vault write -f database/rotate-root/<name>') so that no human knows it.

steps.fake_output:
Key             Value
---             -----
expire_time     2026-09-28T12:41:07Z
id              database/creds/shop-readonly/kQx7TnB2hVp9
issue_time      2026-09-28T11:41:07Z
renewable       true
ttl             58m12s
steps.explanation: 58 minutes left, and it can be renewed.
steps.why: A lease is Vault's promise to clean up. A long-running application renews its lease ('vault lease renew') up to the role's maximum lifetime, then must fetch new credentials and reconnect. Applications that can't handle a credential changing while they run are the main obstacle to adopting dynamic secrets; Vault Agent or the database connection pool usually handles it for them.

steps.prompt: You've finished. Don't wait for the hour: revoke that lease now.
steps.explanation: Vault drops the database user immediately.
steps.why: Revocation is what a static password can't offer: taking access away from one holder, now, without changing it for everyone else.

steps.prompt: A laptop that had used this role was stolen, and you don't know which lease it held. Revoke every credential ever issued from the role shop-readonly.
steps.explanation: Every database user created through that role is dropped.
steps.why: This is the incident-response payoff. With a shared static password, a suspected leak means changing it and redeploying everything that uses it, under pressure. Here it's one command, and running applications simply ask for new credentials. Revoking by prefix is a blunt tool, so know which applications will reconnect before you use it.

steps.prompt:
Dynamic secrets exist for clouds too. What does an AWS secrets engine role give a caller?
  a) The account's root password
  b) A copy of one shared access key
  c) Temporary AWS credentials generated for that request, which expire on their own
  d) Nothing: Vault only handles databases
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
$ vault read aws/creds/deploy
access_key      ASIAEXAMPLEKEY12345
secret_key      (generated)
security_token  (generated)
lease_duration  15m
steps.hint: The same idea as the database user: created on request, short-lived.
steps.explanation: Short-lived credentials minted per request, for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, SSH certificates, and more.
steps.why: The pattern is general: Vault brokers access instead of storing it. Where the platform already has workload identity (identity-tutorial-003), use that first, since it needs no Vault at all. Vault's engines earn their place where identity can't reach directly: databases, on-premises systems, SSH, and third-party APIs.
